title: GTM: General Time-series Model for Representation Learning
one_liner: A time-series model that learns to see patterns at different time-scales by paying attention to frequency information and by practicing both predicting ahead and filling in blanks.
lead: Time-series data (temperature readings, stock prices, sensor streams) has patterns that happen at different speeds. Some patterns repeat every day, others every year. Most time-series models miss these speed differences. GTM fixes this by attending to frequency information — which rhythms are fast, which are slow — and by training on two tasks at once: predicting future values and reconstructing masked (hidden) past values.

problem.h2: Time patterns hide their own speed
paras: Time-series data has patterns at many different scales. A building's temperature changes fast (hour to hour) but also slow (winter to summer). Most models treat time as a flat line: time step 1, 2, 3, 4, 5... They do not know which patterns are hourly hums and which are seasonal shifts.

A beginner's first guess: just use a big neural network on the raw numbers. But the network will ignore that some patterns repeat every 24 time steps and others every 365. It cannot separate the fast signal from the slow signal, so it muddles both together.

callout.html: GTM learns what speed each time pattern runs at by analyzing frequency (which oscillations appear in the data) and by practicing two prediction tasks simultaneously: guessing future values and filling in randomly hidden middle sections.

panels.title: 1. Old way: blind to rhythm
panels.caption: Model sees only raw numbers, treats all time steps the same.

panels.title: 2. Frequency breakdown: fast and slow
panels.caption: The same data contains rhythms at different speeds mixed together.

panels.title: 3. Frequency attention: eyes on each rhythm
panels.caption: Model learns which features capture fast, which capture slow patterns.

panels.title: 4. Two training jobs: guess-ahead AND fill-blanks
panels.caption: Training on both tasks forces the model to hold both types of understanding.

panels.title: 5. Result: robust time sense
panels.caption: Model works well on future prediction, reconstruction, and new downstream tasks.

steps.text: Transform raw time values into frequency space (which rhythms are present and how strong).
Use attention that is aware of time-scale: fast features attend to fast, slow to slow.
Mask out random spans of the time series during training (the model must learn to guess them).
Also train the model to predict the next values in the series (autoregressive task).
Doing both tasks at once forces the model to hold both fast and slow understanding.

object.h2: The single thing that changes: attention weights
paras: Standard attention in time-series models learns what to focus on, but it does not know that some patterns are fast and others slow. GTM changes the attention mechanism so that it explicitly attends to frequency information: how fast is this feature oscillating. The model learns, for each feature, what frequency (speed) it should listen to.

hidden.h2: Time-granularity importance: which speed matters for which feature
hidden.name: frequency-aware importance
paras: Every feature (a learned number that helps predict the time series) tends to specialize: some features pick up on fast changes (hour to hour) and ignore slow drifts, while others do the opposite. This happens because during training, a feature that focuses on one speed gets reinforced by tasks that need that speed, and it gets confused by tasks needing a different speed. The paper introduces a hidden quantity: for each feature, how important are patterns at each frequency. Call it frequency-aware importance. This matters because if a feature is specialized in fast patterns, it should use fast attention weights, and if it is specialized in slow patterns, it should use slow attention weights. Mixing them wastes the feature's capacity.

GTM estimates this by analyzing what happens in the model's attention layer when it processes different speeds of change. Features that grab attention when processing fast oscillations get high importance at high frequencies; features that activate during slow trends get high importance at low frequencies.

heat.caption: Darker means the feature cares more about that speed. Feature-1 watches fast rhythms; Feature-3 watches slow trends; Feature-4 balances all speeds.

reads.html: Think of a stock price: hourly trading noise is fast, quarterly earnings cycles are slow. A good model learns which of its internal features should specialize in noise, which in cycles.

The paper does not name this quantity explicitly, but it is implicit in the frequency-domain attention: each attention head learns to respond to a specific frequency band, ranking how important each frequency is for each feature.

mechanism.h2: Why frequency attention and dual training work
paras: The core problem: a time series is a mix of signals at different speeds, all packed into one number at each time step. A model trained only to predict the next value will learn an average of all those speeds — the fast noise drowns out the slow trend, or the slow trend drowns out the fast noise.

Frequency attention separates the speeds. By explicitly representing each speed (fast frequency, slow frequency) and letting the model learn which internal features care about which speeds, the model builds two separate neural pathways: one for hourly patterns, one for yearly patterns. The model no longer has to jam both into one compressed number.

The dual training (predicting ahead AND filling blanks) forces the model to hold onto both kinds of understanding. If the model cheats and forgets the slow patterns to focus on fast prediction, the reconstruction task (filling blanks) fails — because blanks span both fast and slow scales, and the model must guess correctly at both frequencies.

stages.s: Time series: raw numbers at each time step
Transform to frequency domain: what speeds are present
Frequency-aware attention: each feature learns its preferred speed
Hybrid training: practice both predicting next value and filling blanks
Representation that holds both fast and slow patterns

math.h2: The hybrid loss function that trains on both tasks
math.words: total loss = prediction loss + reconstruction loss. prediction loss = mean square error between guessed next value and true next value. reconstruction loss = mean square error between guessed blanked values and true blanked values.
math.equation: L_total = L_pred + L_recon = mean((y_next - yhat_next)^2) + mean((y_blanked - yhat_blanked)^2)
symbols: the true value that comes after the sequence
the model's guess for the next value
the true values that were randomly hidden during training
the model's guess for what those blanked values were
penalty for getting the prediction wrong
penalty for getting the reconstruction wrong
the combined penalty that training tries to minimize

worked.title: A tiny worked example with three time steps
lines: Say we have a time series: 10, 12, 11, 13. We hide step 3 (the 11). Model guesses next value is 12.5 (true is 13). Model guesses hidden step is 10.8 (true is 11).
Prediction error: (13 - 12.5)^2 = 0.25. Reconstruction error: (11 - 10.8)^2 = 0.04. Total loss: 0.25 + 0.04 = 0.29.
The model is punished for both mistakes equally. It cannot ignore the reconstruction task to perfect the prediction; both matter. This forces it to learn both kinds of patterns.

math.note: The model sees that some mistakes come from missing the fast wiggles (prediction task catches those) and others from missing the slow drifts (reconstruction task catches those), so it learns both.

bars.h2: How GTM performs on different tasks

charts.title: Single-task baseline (predict-only)
charts.note: Model trains only on prediction, so it is good at that but forgets how to fill blanks (the reconstruction signals were never present).

charts.title: GTM (dual-task)
charts.note: Training on both prediction and reconstruction forces the model to learn richer patterns. It is better at all three tasks, including ones it was never specifically trained on, because a model that understands both fast and slow patterns has a more complete picture of how time series behave — any new downstream task only needs subsets of that complete understanding.

items.b: Blanking too much erases the signal.
items.html: If you hide too many consecutive time steps (e.g., hiding steps 10-40 all at once), the model cannot guess what goes in that gap because it is too far from the surrounding context. The reconstruction task becomes impossible, and training fails.

items.b: Frequency mismatch: data without clear rhythms.
items.html: If the time series is pure random noise (no actual patterns at any frequency), frequency-aware attention cannot find anything to specialize in. The model will not fail catastrophically but will gain less advantage from the frequency mechanism than on real, patterned data.

If prediction and reconstruction losses are not roughly equal in magnitude, the model will focus on whichever loss is larger and ignore the other task. Practitioners need to check that both losses are shrinking during training.

Tune the span length for blanking (e.g., hide 10-30% of steps in chunks of 5-10 steps), ensure your data has real patterns at multiple time scales, and monitor both prediction and reconstruction losses to confirm the model is learning both skills.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy time series from scratch: a sine wave with period 50 steps (slow) plus a sine wave with period 5 steps (high-frequency) added together. Train GTM (frequency-aware attention plus dual masking) and a simple baseline (vanilla attention plus prediction-only) on this data. Test on three tasks: predict the next 10 values, fill in 20 randomly blanked values, and classify whether the trend over the last 50 steps was up or down.
demo.closing: GTM should beat the baseline on all three tasks, especially reconstruction (since the baseline never trained on that), proving that dual training and frequency attention build a more complete picture of the time series.
